content.title: About
content.content: Mousse is a light, airy dessert made from whipped egg whites, cream, sugar and flavorings. It can be sweet or savory and is often used in pastry arts to create elegant dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first mousse recipes appeared in France in the 19th century.
There are more than 30 mousse varieties: chocolate, fruit, caramel, cheese and even vegetable.
Gelatin or agar‑agar is often added to achieve the perfect fluffy texture.
Mousse can be served cold or slightly warmed, depending on the recipe.
Traditional chocolate mousse is made without eggs, using only cream and melted chocolate.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Egg whites used in mousse provide a high‑quality source of protein.

items.title: Low in fat (when using reduced‑fat cream)
items.content: Light versions of mousse can be low‑calorie if part of the cream is replaced with reduced‑fat alternatives.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, riboflavin and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Cream used in the recipe is a good source of calcium, supporting bone health.

items.title: Antioxidants from flavorings
items.content: Fruit and chocolate add‑ins are often rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Mousse made with egg whites can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet mousses frequently contain high amounts of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: If not kept at proper temperature, mousse made with raw eggs can become a breeding ground for pathogens.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Classic mousse based on cream contains saturated fats and should be consumed in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve mousse in individual glasses or dessert plates. Pair it with berries, fruit coulis, nuts, chocolate shavings or mint. For a lighter version, use reduced‑fat cream and sugar substitutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared mousse in the refrigerator in a sealed container for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 1 month. Before serving, allow the mousse to thaw slightly and give it a gentle stir.
